findings.subject: pam_pwquality.so
findings.detail: pam_pwquality.so is in the password stack with control 'requisite', so a password that fails its rules is refused. Which rules those are is AUTH-0002's question.

findings.subject: pam_pwquality.so
findings.detail: Password quality requires at least 14 characters (minlen from /etc/security/pwquality.conf:1) and at least 1 digit(s), 1 uppercase letter(s), 1 lowercase letter(s), 1 other character(s) (from /etc/security/pwquality.conf:2).

findings.subject: pam_faillock.so
findings.detail: pam_faillock.so is in the auth stack, so repeated failures are counted and the account is locked. The account locks after 5 failures (/etc/security/faillock.conf:1) for 900 seconds (/etc/security/faillock.conf:2).

findings.subject: pam_unix.so
findings.detail: No pam_unix.so rule accepts an empty password: nullok appears in none of the auth stacks read. An account whose password field is empty is refused rather than admitted.

findings.subject: pam_unix.so
findings.detail: pam_unix.so hashes passwords with yescrypt, so a stolen /etc/shadow is expensive to attack. What is already in the file is USERS-0006's question — the algorithm applies when a password is set, not retroactively.

evidence.excerpt: password [success=1 default=ignore] pam_unix.so obscure use_authtok try_first_pass yescrypt remember=5

findings.subject: pam_pwhistory.so
findings.detail: The last 5 passwords are remembered and refused (remember=5 at /etc/pam.d/common-password:27), so a forced change cannot be satisfied by reusing the password that was being replaced.

evidence.excerpt: password [success=1 default=ignore] pam_unix.so obscure use_authtok try_first_pass yescrypt remember=5

findings.detail: /etc/crontab is owned by root and writable only by root (/etc/crontab (mode 0600, uid 0, gid 0)); no unprivileged account can change what it schedules.
All 5 cron drop-in director(ies) present on this host are owned by root and writable only by root: /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly, /etc/cron.monthly.
/etc/cron.allow exists, so only the users named in it may schedule jobs and access fails closed: an account created later is not on the list and cannot use crontab until somebody adds it.
The cron access-control file(s) present on this host are owned by root and writable only by root: /etc/cron.allow.

All 6 cron path(s) present on this host are readable only by root: /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.hourly, /etc/cron.daily, /etc/cron.weekly, /etc/cron.monthly. What runs as root and when is not disclosed to unprivileged accounts.
All 15 setuid and setgid executables are writable by their owner alone, so nothing but root decides what they run.

All 15 setuid and setgid executables are in the directories a package manager installs into. Whether each of them should carry the bit is a question this check does not answer — it needs package metadata Plumbline does not collect.
No world-writable file was found in 4819 inode(s) examined. Every regular file on this host is writable only by its owner or its group.
All 3 world-writable directories carry the sticky bit, so only a file's own owner may delete or rename it. Whether these directories should be world-writable at all is FILESYS-0005's question.
No directory the operating system depends on is world-writable: nothing under /usr, /etc, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /boot, /opt, /root or /var/lib may be added to by an unprivileged account.
No block or character device node exists outside /dev in 4819 inode(s) examined.

findings.subject: /tmp
findings.detail: /tmp is not a separate mount: it is part of the filesystem mounted at / and inherits its options. nodev, nosuid and noexec are per-mount properties, so a directory that is merely a subdirectory of another filesystem cannot carry them — and /tmp is where anything an unprivileged account brings to the host lands, so it is the one filesystem where removing the ability to execute, to escalate through setuid and to reach a device is worth the inconvenience

evidence.excerpt: no entry for /tmp; the governing mount is / (rw,relatime)

findings.subject: /dev/shm
findings.detail: /dev/shm is a separate tmpfs mount carrying nodev, nosuid, noexec (mounted rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec,relatime).

findings.subject: /home
findings.detail: /home is not a separate mount: it is part of the filesystem mounted at / and inherits its options. nodev, nosuid and noexec are per-mount properties, so a directory that is merely a subdirectory of another filesystem cannot carry them — and home directories are writable by the people who own them, so /home is where a setuid binary or a device node an attacker leaves behind would sit — and nosuid and nodev make both inert without costing any user anything

evidence.excerpt: no entry for /home; the governing mount is / (rw,relatime)

findings.detail: Every owner on this filesystem resolves: 6 distinct uids and 13 distinct gids across 4819 inode(s) examined, and each one is present in /etc/passwd or /etc/group. No file is waiting to be inherited by the next account that takes its number.

findings.subject: kernel.randomize_va_space
findings.detail: kernel.randomize_va_space is 2; the stack, heap, shared libraries and mmap base are all randomised.

findings.subject: kernel.kptr_restrict
findings.detail: kernel.kptr_restrict is 1; kernel pointers are hidden from processes without CAP_SYSLOG.

findings.subject: kernel.yama.ptrace_scope
findings.detail: kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is 1; a process may only attach to its own descendants.

findings.subject: kernel.dmesg_restrict
findings.detail: kernel.dmesg_restrict is 0; any user may read the kernel ring buffer, which exposes kernel addresses and hardware detail useful for building an exploit.

findings.subject: fs.suid_dumpable
findings.detail: fs.suid_dumpable is 0; setuid and setgid programs do not produce core dumps.

findings.subject: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled
findings.detail: kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled is 2; unprivileged bpf() is refused, and the setting may still be raised to 1 to lock it.

No drift was found among the parameters that could be compared, but 1 sysctl configuration file(s) could not be read (/etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf), so a parameter set there may disagree with the running kernel without this check seeing it.

Reverse-path filtering is enabled on all 1 non-loopback interface(s); packets with unroutable source addresses are dropped. eth0 in loose mode (value 2), which accepts a source routable via any interface — correct for asymmetric routing, weaker than strict mode.

findings.subject: fs.protected_symlinks
findings.detail: fs.protected_symlinks is 1; symlinks in world-writable sticky directories are only followed when the follower or the directory owner owns the link.

findings.subject: fs.protected_hardlinks
findings.detail: fs.protected_hardlinks is 1; a hardlink may only be created to a file the user owns or can read and write.

findings.subject: fs.protected_fifos
findings.detail: fs.protected_fifos is 1; an O_CREAT open of another user's FIFO in a world-writable sticky directory is refused.

findings.subject: fs.protected_regular
findings.detail: fs.protected_regular is 2; the restriction covers group-writable sticky directories as well as world-writable ones.

findings.subject: kernel.perf_event_paranoid
findings.detail: kernel.perf_event_paranoid is 2; unprivileged users may not profile the kernel, take CPU-wide measurements, or read raw tracepoints.

findings.subject: kernel.core_pattern
findings.detail: kernel.core_pattern is "core", which is a relative path, so a core dump is written into the crashing process's current working directory. A process that can be induced to run in a writable directory will drop its memory — including credentials and keys — where another user can read it.
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is 0, and an interface accepts source routing only when conf.all and its own setting are both non-zero, so source-routed packets are refused on every interface.

findings.subject: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies
findings.detail: net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is 1; the kernel falls back to SYN cookies when a listening socket's backlog overflows.
All 2 statement(s) setting rsyslog's log file mode restrict it to the owner and a reading group; no account outside that group can read the authentication history.

evidence.excerpt: $FileCreateMode 0640  (legacy-directive syntax; restricts group write and all access by other)
$FileCreateMode 0640  (legacy-directive syntax; restricts group write and all access by other)

findings.detail: 1 remote destination(s) are configured: logs.example.internal over tcp (/etc/rsyslog.d/99-forward.conf:11). A copy of the log leaves this host, so erasing the local file no longer erases the record.

Storage is set to "persistent" at /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/99-hardening.conf:2, so the journal is written to disk and survives a reboot. Note that persistence is not tamper-resistance: the file is still local, and LOGGING-0002 is what puts a copy beyond this host's reach.

evidence.excerpt: Storage=persistent  (the effective value; systemd applies the last occurrence)

findings.detail: ForwardToSyslog is set to "yes" at /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/99-hardening.conf:3, so journald hands its records to rsyslog and rsyslog's own rules decide where they go from there.

evidence.excerpt: ForwardToSyslog=yes  (the effective value; systemd applies the last occurrence)

findings.detail: All 1 remote destination(s) use a reliable transport: logs.example.internal over tcp. Loss is visible rather than silent, and an unreachable collector produces an error on this host rather than nothing at all.
A host firewall is configured: nftables (/etc/nftables.conf). Whether the unit that loads it is enabled is a separate question, which the SERVICES module answers.

evidence.excerpt: nftables configuration, 16 statement(s); type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

findings.detail: The default inbound policy denies: /etc/nftables.conf (type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;). Unmatched inbound traffic is dropped, so a service that starts listening without anybody deciding it should is unreachable until somebody does decide.

evidence.excerpt: nftables configuration, 16 statement(s); type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

findings.detail: One firewall configuration is in force (nftables, /etc/nftables.conf), so the file an operator edits is the one that governs the host.

evidence.excerpt: nftables configuration, 16 statement(s); type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

findings.detail: None of the 23 cleartext-credential units this check knows about is enabled. 23 of them have no unit file on this host.
Neither the mDNS responder, the printer browser nor the RPC portmapper is enabled. 5 of them have no unit file on this host.

findings.subject: systemd-timesyncd.service
findings.detail: systemd-timesyncd.service is enabled and is the only time synchronisation daemon that will start at boot, so nothing competes with it for the clock.
All 70 enablement symlinks resolve to a unit file that exists, so every service an administrator enabled on this host has something for systemd to start.
All 18 unit directories and 240 unit files are owned by root and writable by root alone, so nothing but root decides what starts at boot.
PermitRootLogin is set to no; direct root login over SSH is refused.
PasswordAuthentication is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:2; authentication requires a key, so there is no secret an attacker can guess remotely
PermitEmptyPasswords is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:3; an account with an empty password field is refused rather than admitted
X11Forwarding is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:5; no session can reach a client's X display through this server

MaxAuthTries is set to 3 attempt(s) per connection at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:13; a connection is dropped after a small number of attempts, and a failure is logged early enough for log-based detection to see it

Idle sessions are disconnected after 900 second(s): ClientAliveInterval 300 at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:16 multiplied by ClientAliveCountMax 3 at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:17, within the 900 second limit.

AllowTcpForwarding is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:6; no session can tunnel TCP in either direction, so an account on this host cannot be used to reach past the network boundary it sits behind.

LogLevel is set to "VERBOSE" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:18; authentication outcomes are recorded with the account, source address and method. The key fingerprint is recorded, so a login is attributable to the specific key that authenticated it.

Ciphers at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:20 lists 6 cipher(s) explicitly (chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com, aes256-gcm@openssh.com, aes128-gcm@openssh.com, aes256-ctr, aes192-ctr, aes128-ctr) and none of them is deprecated or broken; every session this host will agree to carry uses a cipher with no known practical attack

MACs at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:21 lists 3 MAC(s) explicitly (hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com, hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com, umac-128-etm@openssh.com) and none of them is deprecated or broken; every session this host will agree to carry is protected by a MAC with no known practical forgery

KexAlgorithms at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:22 lists 5 key exchange(s) explicitly (curve25519-sha256, curve25519-sha256@libssh.org, diffie-hellman-group16-sha512, diffie-hellman-group18-sha512, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256) and none of them is deprecated or broken; every session this host will agree to carry establishes its secret with a method that has no known practical attack
IgnoreRhosts is set to "yes" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:9; the legacy rhosts trust files are not consulted, so a writable home directory cannot grant remote access
HostbasedAuthentication is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:10; authentication requires a credential this user holds rather than a machine they came from
PermitUserEnvironment is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:8; the session environment comes from the system rather than from files the user can write

LoginGraceTime is set to 60 second(s) at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:15; an unauthenticated connection is closed promptly, so the pre-authentication capacity of the listener cannot be held open cheaply

Banner is set to "/etc/issue.net" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:19, so access conditions are presented before authentication. This check does not read that file: whether it exists, and whether its contents leak host details that should not be shown before authentication, are not verified here.
AllowAgentForwarding is set to "no" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:7; no forwarded agent socket is created, so a compromise of this host cannot borrow a user's keys
StrictModes is set to "yes" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:11; a key file that is writable by anyone other than its owner is refused rather than trusted
UsePAM is set to "yes" at /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardening.conf:12; the PAM account and session stack runs, so account expiry, lockout and access policy apply to SSH logins as configured
uid 0 is held by the root account and by no other account in /etc/passwd.
All 20 system account(s) (uid 1-999) have a shell that cannot open a session.
None of the 24 account(s) in /etc/shadow has an empty password field.
All 1 stored password hash(es) use a modern algorithm.
Every one of the 24 account(s) in /etc/passwd has a distinct uid and a distinct name.
/etc/passwd contains no NIS compatibility entries; every account it defines is defined locally.
root holds primary group 0, no ordinary account in /etc/passwd does, and the gid 0 group in /etc/group lists no supplementary members.
Every one of the 46 group(s) in /etc/group has a distinct gid and a distinct name.

All 1 account(s) in /etc/shadow that can authenticate have a maximum password age of 365 days or fewer. Note that NIST SP 800-63B advises against forced rotation, so this PASS reflects the CIS position rather than a universally agreed control.
All 1 account(s) in /etc/shadow that can authenticate have a minimum password age of at least one day, and none has a minimum greater than its maximum.
